documents.title: Diabetes - WHO fact sheet
documents.content: Diabetes is a chronic disease that occurs when the pancreas does not produce enough insulin or the body cannot effectively use the insulin it produces, leading to raised blood sugar (hyperglycaemia). Type 2 diabetes is the most common form and is strongly linked to excess body weight and physical inactivity. Over time uncontrolled diabetes damages blood vessels, the heart, eyes, kidneys and nerves. A healthy diet, regular physical activity, maintaining a normal body weight and avoiding tobacco can prevent or delay type 2 diabetes. Diabetes can be treated and its consequences avoided or delayed with diet, physical activity, medication and regular screening and treatment for complications.

documents.title: About diabetes - CDC
documents.content: Common symptoms of high blood sugar include urinating often, feeling very thirsty, feeling very hungry, blurry vision, numb or tingling hands or feet, very dry skin, sores that heal slowly and unexplained weight loss. Prediabetes means blood sugar levels are higher than normal but not yet high enough for a type 2 diabetes diagnosis; lifestyle changes such as losing a modest amount of weight and being active can lower the risk of progressing. People with risk factors should ask their doctor about a blood sugar test.

documents.title: Hypertension - WHO fact sheet
documents.content: Hypertension (high blood pressure) is when blood pressure is too high, commonly defined as 140/90 mmHg or higher on repeated measurement, although some guidelines use lower thresholds. Most people with hypertension do not feel any symptoms, so measuring blood pressure is the only way to know. Very high blood pressure can cause severe headache, chest pain, dizziness, difficulty breathing, nausea, vision changes, anxiety, confusion or nosebleeds. Modifiable risk factors include diets high in salt and saturated fat, low fruit and vegetable intake, physical inactivity, tobacco and alcohol use, and being overweight. Reducing salt, eating more vegetables and fruit, being active and avoiding tobacco help lower blood pressure.

documents.title: About high blood pressure - CDC
documents.content: High blood pressure usually has no warning signs or symptoms, and many people do not know they have it. It raises the risk of heart disease and stroke. Checking blood pressure regularly, eating a healthy diet low in sodium, getting regular physical activity, keeping a healthy weight, limiting alcohol and not smoking help manage it. People prescribed medicine should take it as directed and work with their healthcare team.

documents.title: Anaemia - WHO fact sheet
documents.content: Anaemia is a condition in which the number of red blood cells or the haemoglobin concentration is lower than normal, reducing the blood's capacity to carry oxygen. Symptoms include fatigue, weakness, dizziness and shortness of breath. Iron deficiency is the most common cause, but other nutritional deficiencies (such as folate and vitamin B12), infections like malaria, chronic inflammation and inherited blood disorders can also cause it. Women of reproductive age, pregnant women and young children are particularly affected. A diet with iron-rich foods and treating underlying causes are key to prevention.

documents.title: Dengue and severe dengue - WHO fact sheet
documents.content: Dengue is a viral infection transmitted to humans through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes. Many infections cause no symptoms; when symptoms occur they commonly include high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pains, nausea, vomiting, swollen glands and rash. Warning signs of severe dengue usually come after the fever goes away and include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, rapid breathing, bleeding gums or nose, fatigue, restlessness, blood in vomit or stool, and being very thirsty; anyone with these signs should get emergency care. There is no specific treatment; care focuses on rest, fluids and pain relief with paracetamol, and medicines such as ibuprofen and aspirin are avoided because they increase bleeding risk.

documents.title: Symptoms of dengue - CDC
documents.content: Dengue symptoms typically last 2 to 7 days and include fever with aches and pains, nausea, vomiting and rash. Warning signs of severe dengue include belly pain or tenderness, vomiting at least three times in 24 hours, bleeding from the nose or gums, vomiting blood or blood in the stool, and feeling tired, restless or irritable. Severe dengue is a medical emergency.

documents.title: Malaria - WHO fact sheet
documents.content: Malaria is a life-threatening disease spread to humans by the bite of infected Anopheles mosquitoes. The first symptoms - fever, headache and chills - usually appear 10 to 15 days after the infective bite and may be mild and difficult to recognise as malaria. Untreated, some forms can progress to severe illness within 24 hours. Early diagnosis by blood test and prompt treatment reduce disease and prevent deaths. Prevention includes insecticide-treated nets and other vector control.

documents.title: Typhoid - WHO fact sheet
documents.content: Typhoid fever is a life-threatening infection caused by Salmonella Typhi, usually spread through contaminated food or water. Symptoms include prolonged high fever, fatigue, headache, nausea, abdominal pain and constipation or diarrhoea; some patients have a rash. It is treated with antibiotics, although resistance is increasing. Safe water, sanitation, hand hygiene and vaccination help prevent it.

documents.title: Tuberculosis - WHO fact sheet
documents.content: Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by bacteria that most often affect the lungs and spreads through the air when people with TB cough, sneeze or spit. Common symptoms include a prolonged cough (sometimes with blood), chest pain, weakness, fatigue, weight loss, fever and night sweats. TB is preventable and curable with a course of antibiotics taken under medical supervision. People with these symptoms, particularly a cough lasting more than two weeks, should be tested.

documents.title: About tuberculosis - CDC
documents.content: TB disease symptoms can include a bad cough lasting three weeks or longer, chest pain, coughing up blood or sputum, weakness or fatigue, weight loss, no appetite, chills, fever and night sweats. TB can be treated by taking medicine exactly as prescribed for the full course.

documents.title: Influenza (seasonal) - WHO fact sheet
documents.content: Seasonal influenza is an acute respiratory infection caused by influenza viruses. Symptoms begin suddenly and include fever, cough (usually dry), headache, muscle and joint pain, severe malaise, sore throat and runny nose. Most people recover within a week without medical care, but influenza can cause severe illness in high-risk groups such as pregnant women, young children, older adults and people with chronic medical conditions. Annual vaccination is the most effective prevention.

documents.title: Signs and symptoms of flu - CDC
documents.content: Flu often comes on suddenly with fever or feeling feverish, chills, cough, sore throat, runny or stuffy nose, muscle or body aches, headaches and fatigue. Emergency warning signs in adults include difficulty breathing or shortness of breath, persistent chest or abdominal pain or pressure, persistent dizziness or confusion, seizures, severe weakness, and symptoms that improve then return with fever and worse cough.

documents.title: Coronavirus disease (COVID-19) - WHO fact sheet
documents.content: COVID-19 is caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Common symptoms include fever, chills, sore throat, cough, fatigue, muscle aches and loss of taste or smell. Most people experience mild to moderate illness and recover without special treatment, but older people and those with underlying conditions are more likely to develop serious illness. Anyone with difficulty breathing, chest pain, confusion or loss of speech or mobility should seek immediate care.

documents.title: Symptoms of COVID-19 - CDC
documents.content: COVID-19 symptoms may appear 2 to 14 days after exposure and include fever or chills, cough, shortness of breath, fatigue, muscle or body aches, headache, new loss of taste or smell, sore throat, congestion, nausea and diarrhoea. Seek emergency care for trouble breathing, persistent chest pain or pressure, new confusion, inability to wake or stay awake, or pale, gray or blue-coloured skin, lips or nail beds.

documents.title: Asthma - WHO fact sheet
documents.content: Asthma is a chronic lung disease in which the airways become inflamed and narrowed. Symptoms include cough, wheeze, shortness of breath and chest tightness, often worse at night or with exercise, and they can vary over time. Triggers include viral infections, allergens, tobacco smoke, air pollution and cold air. Inhaled medications can control symptoms and allow people to lead normal, active lives; avoiding triggers also helps.

documents.title: About asthma - CDC
documents.content: Asthma affects the airways that carry air to and from the lungs. Common symptoms are coughing, wheezing, chest tightness and shortness of breath. People with asthma can manage it with an asthma action plan developed with their doctor, by taking medicines as prescribed and by avoiding triggers.

documents.title: Pneumonia - WHO fact sheet
documents.content: Pneumonia is a form of acute respiratory infection that affects the lungs, where the air sacs fill with pus and fluid, making breathing painful and limiting oxygen intake. It can be caused by viruses, bacteria or fungi. Symptoms include cough, fever, fast or difficult breathing and chest pain. Bacterial pneumonia is treated with antibiotics prescribed by a clinician; vaccination, adequate nutrition and reducing indoor air pollution help prevent it.

documents.title: Diarrhoeal disease - WHO fact sheet
documents.content: Diarrhoea is the passage of three or more loose or liquid stools per day. It is usually a symptom of a gut infection spread through contaminated food or drinking water or from person to person due to poor hygiene. The most severe threat is dehydration, which is prevented and treated with oral rehydration salts (ORS) solution. Zinc supplements help in children. Safe drinking water, sanitation and hand washing with soap reduce the risk.

documents.title: About norovirus - CDC
documents.content: Norovirus is a very contagious virus that causes vomiting and diarrhoea, often with nausea and stomach pain, and sometimes fever, headache and body aches. Most people get better within one to three days. Drinking plenty of liquids to replace fluid lost helps prevent dehydration; signs of dehydration include decreased urination, dry mouth and throat, and feeling dizzy when standing.

documents.title: Headache disorders - WHO fact sheet
documents.content: Headache disorders, such as migraine and tension-type headache, are among the most common disorders of the nervous system. Migraine typically causes recurrent, moderate to severe pulsating headache, often on one side, with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound, lasting hours to days. Tension-type headache is often described as pressure or tightness around the head. Lifestyle factors, regular sleep and identifying triggers help, and effective treatments are available from healthcare providers. Sudden, severe or unusual headaches need urgent medical assessment.

documents.title: Cardiovascular diseases - WHO fact sheet
documents.content: Cardiovascular diseases are a group of disorders of the heart and blood vessels and are a leading cause of death globally. The most important behavioural risk factors are unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, tobacco use and harmful use of alcohol, which can show up as raised blood pressure, raised blood glucose, raised blood lipids and overweight. Symptoms of a heart attack include pain or discomfort in the centre of the chest and in the arms, left shoulder, elbows, jaw or back, along with difficulty breathing, nausea, light-headedness or cold sweat. Symptoms of a stroke include sudden weakness of the face, arm or leg, often on one side, confusion, difficulty speaking, vision problems and loss of balance. These need emergency care.

documents.title: Heart attack symptoms - CDC
documents.content: Major symptoms of a heart attack are chest pain or discomfort, feeling weak, light-headed or faint, a cold sweat, pain or discomfort in the jaw, neck or back, pain in one or both arms or shoulders, and shortness of breath. Women may also have unusual tiredness and nausea or vomiting. If you think someone is having a heart attack, call emergency services right away.

documents.title: Stroke signs and symptoms - CDC
documents.content: Signs of stroke include sudden numbness or weakness in the face, arm or leg, especially on one side of the body; sudden confusion, trouble speaking or understanding speech; sudden trouble seeing; sudden trouble walking, dizziness or loss of balance; and sudden severe headache with no known cause. Act F.A.S.T.: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call emergency services. Note the time symptoms started.

documents.title: About cholesterol - CDC
documents.content: High cholesterol usually has no symptoms, so a blood test is the only way to know. LDL cholesterol raises the risk of heart disease and stroke, while HDL helps carry cholesterol back to the liver. Eating a healthy diet low in saturated fat, getting regular physical activity, keeping a healthy weight and not smoking help manage cholesterol; some people also need medicine prescribed by their doctor.

documents.title: About chronic kidney disease - CDC
documents.content: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) means the kidneys are damaged and cannot filter blood as well as they should. Early CKD often has no symptoms, so testing with blood and urine tests is the only way to know. Diabetes and high blood pressure are the most common causes. Managing blood sugar and blood pressure, staying active, eating a healthy diet and avoiding unnecessary use of medicines that can harm the kidneys help slow progression.

documents.title: About urinary tract infections - CDC
documents.content: Urinary tract infections are common infections that happen when bacteria enter the urinary tract. Bladder infection symptoms include pain or burning while urinating, frequent urination, feeling the need to urinate despite an empty bladder, bloody urine and pressure or cramping in the lower abdomen. Fever, back or side pain below the ribs, nausea or vomiting can mean the infection has reached the kidneys and needs prompt care. A healthcare professional can test urine and decide whether antibiotics are needed.

documents.title: Hepatitis B - WHO fact sheet
documents.content: Hepatitis B is a viral infection that attacks the liver and can cause both acute and chronic disease. Some people have acute illness with yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice), dark urine, extreme fatigue, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain. It is transmitted through contact with infected body fluids. A safe and effective vaccine is available, and chronic infection can be managed with medicines.

documents.title: About viral hepatitis - CDC
documents.content: Hepatitis means inflammation of the liver. It is often caused by a virus, but heavy alcohol use, certain medications and some medical conditions can also cause it. Many people with viral hepatitis do not have symptoms; when present, symptoms can include fever, fatigue, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dark urine, light-coloured stools, joint pain and jaundice. Blood tests are used to diagnose it.

documents.title: Obesity and overweight - WHO fact sheet
documents.content: For adults, WHO defines overweight as a body mass index (BMI) of 25 or more and obesity as a BMI of 30 or more. Overweight and obesity increase the risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, some cancers and musculoskeletal disorders. Healthy diets and regular physical activity, supported by healthy environments, are the foundations of prevention and management.

documents.title: Physical activity - WHO fact sheet
documents.content: WHO recommends that adults do at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity, or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity, per week, plus muscle-strengthening activities on two or more days. Regular physical activity helps prevent and manage heart disease, type 2 diabetes and some cancers, reduces symptoms of depression and anxiety, and improves wellbeing. Doing some physical activity is better than doing none.

documents.title: Physical activity guidelines for adults - CDC
documents.content: Adults need at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity physical activity, such as brisk walking, each week and at least two days of muscle-strengthening activity. Activity can be spread through the week in shorter sessions.

documents.title: Healthy diet - WHO fact sheet
documents.content: A healthy diet includes fruits, vegetables, legumes, nuts and whole grains, with at least 400 g of fruit and vegetables a day. WHO advises limiting free sugars to less than 10% of total energy intake, keeping salt intake below 5 g per day, and limiting saturated and trans fats. A healthy diet helps protect against malnutrition and noncommunicable diseases such as diabetes, heart disease and stroke.

documents.title: Micronutrient facts - CDC
documents.content: Micronutrients such as iron, vitamin D, vitamin A, folate, iodine and zinc are needed in small amounts but are essential for health. Iron is needed for growth and development, and iron deficiency is a leading cause of anaemia. Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium for bone health. A varied diet supports adequate intake; some people may need supplements as advised by a healthcare professional.

documents.title: Tobacco - WHO fact sheet
documents.content: Tobacco kills up to half of its users and is a major risk factor for cardiovascular and respiratory diseases and many cancers. Second-hand smoke also causes serious disease. Quitting at any age brings health benefits, and support such as counselling, quit lines and medicines can double the chances of success.

documents.title: Depressive disorder - WHO fact sheet
documents.content: Depression is a common mental disorder involving a depressed mood or loss of pleasure or interest in activities for long periods of time. Other symptoms include poor concentration, feelings of excessive guilt or low self-worth, hopelessness, thoughts about dying or suicide, disrupted sleep, changes in appetite or weight, and feeling very tired. Effective psychological treatments and, in some cases, medicines are available. Anyone having thoughts of self-harm should reach out to a health professional or crisis service immediately.

documents.title: Suicide - WHO fact sheet
documents.content: Suicide is preventable. Early identification, support and follow-up for people in distress, and limiting access to means, are effective interventions. Anyone in immediate danger should contact local emergency services or a crisis helpline, and talking to a trusted person or health professional can help.
